Granola publishes a downloadable OpenAPI 3.1 document ("Granola API", server https://public-api.granola.ai; /v1 endpoints for notes, transcripts, folders, spaces, audit, webhook-endpoints, and legal holds), advertised in the docs llms.txt under "OpenAPI Specs". Gate caveat: "Any workspace member on a **Business** or **Enterprise** plan can create API keys."

The Mintlify-hosted API reference runs the interactive playground ("Try it" button sending live requests to https://public-api.granola.ai with a bearer key): "The Granola API provides programmatic access to your workspace's meeting notes and related data. This RESTful API enables you to integrate Granola with your existing tools, build custom workflows, and extract insights from your meeting documentation." Rate limits: "API keys are rate limited to 25 requests burst capacity with a sustained rate of 5 requests/second."

Counter-check: Granola answers the sandbox question directly in its API FAQ: "Is there a sandbox or test environment?" — "Not currently. We recommend testing with a small number of notes in a dedicated test folder."

The API is /v1 path-versioned with a dated, semantically versioned API changelog (v1.0.0 through v1.6.0, each entry listing endpoint and response changes, e.g. "**Get Note** now returns `413 TRANSCRIPT_TOO_LARGE` when a transcript cannot be returned inline."). No deprecation window or back-compat commitment is published (zero deprecation/backward-compatibility text in the docs corpus).

A user who installed the Granola Apple Watch app found that phone call recording works by putting you in the middle: you place the call to the other party through it. They called it an interesting solution.
A beta tester of Granola for Apple Watch said it is not bad for watch battery life at all and "works like a charm."

"Granola terrifies me. It's highly capable at summarisation, and seems to be free. What's the catch?" The user worries that it runs in the background on their Mac with access to their microphone, calendar data and private meeting notes.
Granola is only free for a limited number of notes. You could copy-paste the summaries into Obsidian, but at that point you're better off using local tools like MacParakeet or OpenWhispr.

One user liked the Apple Watch strap and thought a watch app is a great idea for this, but couldn't bring themselves to try "ANOTHER meeting notetaker app." They find the space commoditised and asked how Granola differs from Fireflies or the many others.
A user wants something like Granola for Apple Watch, but with local (iPhone) or self-hosted processing using whisper/parakeet, instead of cloud processing.

A PM with many calls said action items from Granola tended to slip through. As a workaround, they built a Mac app that turns Granola calls into a kanban to-do list, with each action item attached to its full meeting transcript and data stored locally as .md files.
Current Granola user who had wanted to build an open-source alternative himself; plans to try Hyprnote, which fine-tunes a small local model for meeting summarization.

User says hosted/online notetakers such as Granola, Notion recorder and ChatGPT recorder 'don't really make sense if you can record locally', so they are trying a local, open-source alternative instead.
